turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, give me a second, it just kicked me back to the login screen. Okay. You're in for the repeats, but say again what you wanted. I only half caught it at the door.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): The repeats, yes, but the real reason is my right knee. It's a deep ache, worse on the stairs, stiff for about twenty minutes every morning, and I wake at night to shift it. Walking the dog loosens it, and a bag of ice helps a little. I came hoping you might give me something stronger than what I'm already on.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee. How long has it been like that? One more time, I was in the wrong chart.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I almost said three months. No, scratch that, it's been five months, since around the new year, because I remember not being able to kneel down and fix the cabinet hinge in the kitchen.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five months. Any swelling, or does it give out under you?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling, and it doesn't give out. My wife looks at it every night like she's going to find something, and there's never anything puffy. I keep telling her she's worrying over a knee that's just loud and sore.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Pharmacy list is up whenever you want the doses. I can't print it, the printer's jammed again, so we'll just read off the screen.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks. What are you actually taking for the knee? Go slow, this page keeps jumping.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Naproxen, five hundred milligrams, one tablet twice a day, by mouth, with food, for the knee. Breakfast and dinner. I don't skip that one, I even set the bottle by the coffee maker so I see it.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): What I have on the pharmacy list is naproxen two hundred fifty milligrams twice a day. Not five hundred.

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): That doesn't match the bottle in my cabinet. I read it this morning, orange label, five hundred milligrams, sitting right next to the coffee. I've been looking at that bottle for months.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't, uh, don't re-litigate it while the chart's frozen. We'll leave the naproxen exactly as it is. No dose change from me today.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still using Tylenol with it? Say the strength, I don't trust what I half typed.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Five hundred milligrams, no, sorry, I always mix that up with the regular extra strength. They're the eight-hour arthritis ones, six hundred and fifty milligrams, two tablets three times a day when the knee is bad, by mouth. On a quiet yard day I might not take any.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two of the six-fifty, up to three times, only when it's bad. And the stomach pill? I just typed twenty by mistake, ignore that. What do you take?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty milligrams, no, that's the old dose. It's forty milligrams of omeprazole every morning, by mouth, for my stomach, because of the naproxen. You raised it a while back and I tossed the twenty bottle.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Every morning, though? You actually get it in every morning?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. If I'm rushing out to the hardware store I skip it, so don't put down that I'm perfect with it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Sort of noted. Blood pressure pill still the same? Repeat it, I lost the line.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, ten milligrams, every morning, by mouth, for my blood pressure. I don't miss that one. The pressure problem's been going on for years, and I line that pill up before the omeprazole, ironically.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Lisinopril ten daily matches our list. Omeprazole forty matches too. Naproxen is the only one that doesn't.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies? The alert bar still isn't loading, so I have to ask out loud.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. Penicillin was fine when I had that tooth, and there's nothing else.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The tooth was a whole picnic disaster, temporary crown popped off into the potato salad at my nephew's graduation, everybody staring, but that is not why I came and I should stop.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yeah, skip the potato salad. What stronger medicine were you picturing, exactly?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Hydrocodone, the Norco my neighbor has, five-three-twenty-five. Just a small number for the nights and the stairs, not to take every day. He says they wipe out his back pain, and his back sounds worse than my knee, so I thought a few wouldn't be crazy.

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. I'm not prescribing hydrocodone. This still sounds like your knee osteoarthritis acting up, and a narcotic isn't the right tool, especially with those Norco tablets also carrying acetaminophen while you're already on Tylenol.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I figured you'd say no. They told me osteoarthritis after the arthroscopy, that was twenty nineteen, they trimmed the meniscus in the right knee. So that diagnosis is already on the books, it's not something new I made up today.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, the old scope. I'm not ordering an x-ray. Nothing you're describing sounds like a fresh injury.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any burning in the stomach, or black stools, on the naproxen?

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No burning, and no black stools. I check, which is probably more information than you wanted about my bathroom. The ice I do with a bag of frozen peas most evenings after the dog.

[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the ice after the longer walks. Don't put any other anti-inflammatory on top of the naproxen, no drugstore ibuprofen. Stay with the Tylenol the way you said, two of the six-fifty when the knee is bad, and don't go past that in a day.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't buy ibuprofen, and I won't take the neighbor's Norco even if he offers it out of that kitchen drawer. That's his mess. I'll stick to the peas and the pills you already know about.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. I'll renew the lisinopril ten milligrams and the omeprazole forty milligrams the way they are. I'm not touching the naproxen until your bottle and that list say the same strength.

[SEG0035] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can leave a note for the pharmacist that naproxen needs a strength check, two fifty on our list versus five hundred on his bottle. I won't rewrite the label myself.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, leave that note. Come back in six weeks for another med check. If the knee suddenly locks or swells up hard before then, don't wait it out, call us.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, I can do that. I'll bring the actual naproxen bottle so nobody has to argue from memory, and I'll keep walking the dog, just slower on the way back up the hill.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring the bottle, yes, that'll help. I have to reboot this machine before the next chart. We're finished for today.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll walk you toward the pharmacy window and drop that note in. Watch the mat by the door, it's curled up.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Appreciate it. If the computer eats the renewals, I'll call, but I think I followed everything, even the part where I don't get the stronger pills.
